narrative:
The model predicted a 67% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your undergraduate GPA, your first-year law school grades, and your LSAT score. Your undergraduate GPA was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. At 2.80 it sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of students who were accepted, signaling weaker academic preparation. Your first-year law school performance ranked second in importance and also pulled the outcome toward failure; you placed in the third decile compared with an average of sixth decile among accepted students. These two academic signals together created a clear picture of elevated risk.

Your LSAT score of 40 worked in the opposite direction. It is higher than the 37.18 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward passing, but not enough to overcome the academic concerns.

Taken together, the model concluded that the combination of lower grades in college and early law school made success on the bar exam less likely, despite a solid LSAT result.

What you should do next is strengthen the areas the model flagged. Retake challenging courses to raise your GPA, seek targeted academic support during law school, and consider retaking the LSAT if you can improve it further. With clearer evidence of stronger academic performance, a future application would have a much better chance. (248 words)
